title: Young stellar jet MHO 1502
caption: The young stellar jet MHO 1502, imaged by the Gemini South telescope
credit: International Gemini Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA · Acknowledgments: · Image processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) & D. de Martin (NSF NOIRLab)PI: L. Ferrero (Universidad Nacional de Córdoba)

recognition.text: Official NSF NOIRLab / Gemini press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: A knotted jet of gas stretches through this infrared image of MHO 1502, a young stellar jet captured from Chile by the international Gemini Observatory. The jet is embedded in an H II region, an area of star formation where hydrogen gas is lit up by young stars, in the direction of Vela.

The jet is bipolar, streaming out in two opposite directions, and it is made of a chain of knots. That pattern suggests its source, which is thought to be a pair of stars, has been emitting material in fits and starts rather than steadily, with each knot perhaps marking a separate outburst.

The crisp detail comes from Gemini South's adaptive optics system, which helps counteract the blurring caused by turbulence in Earth's atmosphere. Young stars often launch jets like this while they are still growing, and the jets can carry material far out into the surrounding cloud. The object listing for this image also includes DGL 4.

understand.summary: A near-infrared image from the GSAOI instrument on Gemini South, using adaptive optics, through a molecular hydrogen (H2) filter and a broadband filter; the colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, so the colours here are a translation of light we cannot see.
